title: Lists in Python
relevance: Lists are the default mutable sequence in Python OAs and SDE interviews; candidates must know storage, mutation APIs, and comprehension patterns.

phases.goal: Establish what a Python list is and the core properties that distinguish it from fixed arrays.

must_hit.point: A list stores multiple items under one name and behaves as a dynamic array that can grow as items are added.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Says lists hold many values under one variable and can resize when you add items.

must_hit.point: Lists are ordered, mutable, allow heterogeneous types and duplicates, can be nested, and support indexing/slicing.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Lists key traits: order preserved, editable after creation, mixed types OK, duplicates OK, nesting OK, index/slice access.

must_hit.point: Compared to arrays: lists are dynamic and heterogeneous; arrays are fixed-size and homogeneous, and arrays are faster with contiguous allocation while lists use referential arrays.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Contrasts size, data types, speed, and memory layout between arrays and lists.

probes: What is a Python list, and how does it differ from a traditional array on size and element types?

hints.1: Start from the idea of one name holding many values.
hints.2: Contrast fixed vs dynamic size and same-type vs mixed-type storage.
hints.3: Lists are dynamic heterogeneous referential arrays; classical arrays are fixed, homogeneous, contiguous, and faster.

phases.goal: Explain referential storage, resize-on-growth, and the main mutation/access APIs.

must_hit.point: Python lists are referential arrays: each slot holds a memory address to an object, not the object's value inline, which is why heterogeneous contents work.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes pointers/addresses in the list pointing to objects elsewhere; addresses are fixed-size so types can differ.

must_hit.point: When a list runs out of space, Python allocates a larger block (usually double), copies existing references, adds the new item, then deletes the old array.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Walks the grow steps: bigger block, copy refs, append, free old storage.

must_hit.point: append adds one item at the end (a passed list becomes one nested element); extend adds each item from an iterable; insert places one item at a given index.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Distinguishes append nesting vs extend flattening vs insert-at-index.

must_hit.point: Deletion uses del (index/slice/whole variable), remove (first matching value), pop (by index, returns item; last if no index), and clear (empties to []).
must_hit.evidence_hint: Names the four removal tools and what each targets.

must_hit.point: sort and reverse mutate in place; sorted returns a new sorted list without modifying the original; copy returns a shallow copy.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Separates in-place methods from sorted()/copy() that produce another list.

probes: How is a Python list stored in memory, and what happens internally when it needs to grow?
How do append, extend, and insert differ when adding items?

hints.1: Think locker maps versus stuffing values directly in the lockers.
hints.2: Cover referential slots, then the allocate-copy-add-delete resize path, then the three add APIs.
hints.3: List holds addresses; growth usually doubles then copies refs; append nests a whole list, extend unpacks an iterable, insert takes an index.

phases.goal: Surface flexibility costs of lists versus arrays and versus safer copying patterns.

must_hit.point: Lists trade speed and memory for flexibility: slower than arrays, and they use extra reserved space plus references rather than packing raw values.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Mentions slower execution and higher memory from over-allocation and reference storage.

must_hit.point: Arbitrary insertion/deletion on lists is O(n), so lists are flexible but costly for middle-of-list edits.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Calls out O(n) for arbitrary insert/delete as a downside.

must_hit.point: Mutability plus aliasing is risky: assignment like b = a shares one list object, so mutating through one name changes the other.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Explains shared identity after assignment and that append on one name shows up on the other.

probes: What are the main disadvantages of Python lists compared with arrays or more careful sharing?

hints.1: Flexibility usually costs something in speed or memory.
hints.2: Tie costs to over-allocation, references, and O(n) middle edits, plus shared mutable aliases.
hints.3: Lists are slower and memory-heavier; middle insert/delete is O(n); b = a aliases so both see the same mutations.

phases.goal: Apply list building, comprehensions, membership nuance, and multi-list iteration in concrete snippets.

must_hit.point: List comprehension replaces an empty-list-plus-append loop with [expression for item in iterable if condition], and is described as more time- and space-efficient than an equivalent Python loop.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Shows bracket form with optional filter and says it beats the manual append loop on efficiency.

must_hit.point: Membership checks the top-level list only: for L2 = [1, 2, 3, 4, [5, 6]], [5, 6] in L2 is True but 5 in L2 is False.
must_hit.evidence_hint: Uses nested-list membership example: whole sublist found, bare 5 not found.

must_hit.point: zip pairs items from multiple lists so you can operate indexwise, e.g. [i + j for i, j in zip(L1, L2)].
must_hit.evidence_hint: Describes zip aggregating iterables into pairs used in a comprehension.

probes: Rewrite a loop that appends values into a list comprehension, and explain when membership fails on a nested value.
How would you add two lists indexwise with zip?

hints.1: Compress the create-empty-list then append pattern into one bracket expression.
hints.2: Mention the if-filter form, then nested membership, then zip for parallel lists.
hints.3: [expr for x in it if cond]; 5 is not in a list that only nests [5, 6] at top level; zip(L1, L2) then combine pair elements.

tradeoffs.strong_answer: Arrays are fixed-size, homogeneous, contiguous, and faster; lists are dynamic, heterogeneous, referential, and slower but far more flexible for mixed data and growth.
Both build lists the same way logically; comprehension is a compressed form optimized at the C level and is more time- and space-efficient with fewer lines.
append adds one object (a list argument becomes one nested element); extend iterates an iterable and adds each element individually—including characters if given a string.
b = a shares one mutable list so edits via a appear on b; copy() makes a shallow separate list object to avoid that aliasing side effect.

gotchas.trap: Assuming append([6, 7, 8]) flattens those numbers onto the list.
gotchas.correction: append adds the whole list as a single nested element; use extend to add 6, 7, and 8 individually.

gotchas.trap: Thinking extend('delhi') adds the string 'delhi' as one item.
gotchas.correction: extend walks the string and appends each character separately.
in only checks top-level elements; 5 lives inside a nested list, so the check is False while [5, 6] in that list is True.

gotchas.trap: Assuming b = a copies the list so later appends on a leave b unchanged.
gotchas.correction: Assignment aliases the same list object; both names see the mutation unless you copy.
sort and reverse mutate in place; sorted returns a new sorted list and leaves the original unchanged.
